description: Working solo on the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map
summary:
Marswalk Planner is a free web map of Jezero Crater on Mars for planning a walk on foot. You place a base and draw a route, and it gives a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict with its reasons, the time out and back, a turn-back point, and the science stops along the way.

It addresses the Martian Map challenge by bringing together imagery and elevation from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Global Surveyor, Mars Express, Mars Odyssey and Perseverance on one map of a real landing site, turning them into one answer: does a planned walk stay within the slope and time limits? Slopes come from a 40 m grid made from the USGS CTX elevation model. Compared with 708 points on Perseverance's route, it differs by about 3 m (3.1 m RMS).

This matters because whether a walk stays within its limits depends on slope, distance and time together, and that data is spread across several missions. The planner puts it in one view and shows every reason for its verdict. The limits, walking speed and time budget are labelled as our assumptions, not NASA's. It is a student project, not endorsed by NASA or for real mission planning.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Marswalk Planner is a free web map of Jezero Crater on Mars. Place a base and draw a route, and it reports the distance, an elevation profile, the steepest slope and where it is, the walking time out and back, and a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict that lists every reason. Under the Standard assumptions, a slope over 15° or a time margin under 25% is a Caution, and a slope over 25°, running over the time budget, or leaving the elevation data is a No-Go. The 4.83 km demo walk gets a CAUTION at 18.1°. One step further up the delta scarp makes it a NO-GO at 26.7°.

HOW IT WORKS

It runs entirely in the browser. Map tiles come from NASA Mars Trek, shown with the Leaflet library. Every slope is measured in 50 m steps on a 40 m elevation grid averaged from the USGS Mars 2020 CTX elevation model. Walking speed follows the Tobler hiking function from an assumed 3.5 km/h, within an assumed 8-hour budget. Features include Play the walk (a replay with live slope, speed and time), a turn-back point, a safest-route search, a check of all nine Perseverance sample stops, and the rover's own path coloured by slope.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

It puts slope, distance, time and science stops from several missions in one view, explains every verdict, and links every number to its source in SOURCES.md. It is free and needs no sign-in. The aim is to show how open NASA data can give a clear, checkable answer to a planning question, with its limits just as clear. Next steps: live conditions if an official feed appears, sun angle and shadows along a route, and suit and oxygen models built only from published data.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript as a static site, Leaflet 1.9.4, Python and Node.js scripts to build the data, 294 Node.js unit tests, and GitHub Pages. No special hardware. AI coding assistance was used (see the SI section). Open source under the Apache License 2.0.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It turns map layers into a decision about one specific walk, and Play the walk lets you watch that walk happen. It uses the rover as a test: the elevation grid is checked against 708 points on Perseverance's route (about 3 m typical difference), and the rover's path is coloured by slope to ask whether a person could walk where it drove. The assumptions (Cautious, Standard, Ambitious or your own numbers) change the verdict straight away.

FACTORS I CONSIDERED

Never inventing data: every number cites a source or is labelled as an assumption, and the limits are this project's, not NASA's. Honest limits: slopes are averaged over about 50 m, so short steep steps and boulders do not show, and the walking model was made for Earth, with no fatigue, suit mass or Mars-gravity effect. Ease of use: plain names, a Why? button and a 60-second guided tour. Phones and accessibility: tested on a real phone, with keyboard support and a reduced-motion mode. It is a student project, not for real mission planning.
dataRefs: NASA Mars Trek map tiles and layers
NASA Mars Trek tile service (WMTS API)
Mars 2020 CTX DEM mosaic of Jezero Crater, 20 m (USGS, from MRO CTX images)
HiRISE imagery, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (NASA/JPL/University of Arizona)
MOLA elevation and shaded relief, Mars Global Surveyor (NASA/GSFC)
THEMIS day and night infrared, Mars Odyssey (NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU)
Hydrous mineral detections, CRISM and OMEGA (NASA Mars Trek layer)
Perseverance waypoints data, used for the 708-point elevation check (NASA/JPL-Caltech)
MEDA weather data, Mars 2020 (NASA PDS Atmospheres Node)
Curiosity REMS weather feed (NASA/JPL-Caltech, REMS team)
RAD surface radiation, Curiosity (NASA/JPL news release)
Herd et al. 2023, Mars 2020 sample overview (NASA Technical Reports Server)
projectRefs: ESA Mars Express HRSC elevation, in the MOLA + HRSC layer via NASA Mars Trek (ESA/DLR/FU Berlin)
ESA Mars Express OMEGA mineral detections, via NASA Mars Trek (ESA/IAS)
MEDA results: Rodriguez-Manfredi et al. 2023, Nature Geoscience (CC BY 4.0)
Tobler hiking function: Tobler 1993 (walking speed model)
Full source list with licences and credit lines (SOURCES.md)
